claim: MT and V4 are mid-tier stages of the dorsal and ventral pathways, respectively.
source: MT and V4 are counterpart mid-tier stages of the dorsal and ventral pathways, both of which causally contribute to stereoscopic depth judgment (DeAngelis et al., 1998; Shiozaki et al., 2012; Uka and DeAngelis, 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies showing that MT and V4 causally contribute to stereoscopic depth judgment, supporting their characterization as mid-tier stages.

claim: MT and V4 both causally contribute to stereoscopic depth judgment.
source: MT and V4 are counterpart mid-tier stages of the dorsal and ventral pathways, both of which causally contribute to stereoscopic depth judgment (DeAngelis et al., 1998; Shiozaki et al., 2012; Uka and DeAngelis, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three previous studies demonstrating causal contributions of MT and V4 to stereoscopic depth judgment.

claim: MT neurons transmitted disparity signals more quickly than V4 neurons.
source: We found that MT neurons transmitted disparity signals more quickly and robustly, whereas V4 or its upstream neurons transformed the signals into sophisticated representations more prominently.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figure 8 showing latency differences.

claim: MT neurons transmitted disparity signals more robustly than V4 neurons.
source: We found that MT neurons transmitted disparity signals more quickly and robustly, whereas V4 or its upstream neurons transformed the signals into sophisticated representations more prominently.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figure 8 showing amplitude differences.

claim: V4 neurons transformed disparity signals into sophisticated representations more prominently than MT neurons.
source: We found that MT neurons transmitted disparity signals more quickly and robustly, whereas V4 or its upstream neurons transformed the signals into sophisticated representations more prominently.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing differences in area ratios between MT and V4, indicating different types of disparity representations.

claim: Signaling speed and robustness were traded for transformation between the dorsal and ventral pathways.
source: Therefore, signaling speed and robustness were traded for transformation between the dorsal and ventral pathways.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined findings that MT has faster/stronger signals while V4 has more sophisticated representations.

claim: V4 neurons had more even-symmetric tuning than MT neurons.
source: The key factor in this tradeoff was disparity-tuning shape: V4 neurons had more even-symmetric tuning than MT neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7 comparing the distributions of reflected symmetry phase between MT and V4.

claim: Tuning symmetry predicted the degree of signal transformation across neurons within each area.
source: Moreover, the tuning symmetry predicted the degree of signal transformation across neurons similarly within each area, implying a general role of tuning symmetry in the stereoscopic processing by the two pathways.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6 demonstrating correlations between tuning symmetry and area ratio within MT and V4.

claim: The dorsal pathway is implicated in spatial vision and vision for action.
source: In the visual systems of human and non-human primates, the dorsal pathway is implicated in spatial vision and vision for action, whereas the ventral pathway is implicated in object recognition and vision for perception (Goodale and Milner, 1992; Ungerleider and Mishkin, 1982).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational studies on the dorsal and ventral pathways.

claim: The ventral pathway is implicated in object recognition and vision for perception.
source: In the visual systems of human and non-human primates, the dorsal pathway is implicated in spatial vision and vision for action, whereas the ventral pathway is implicated in object recognition and vision for perception (Goodale and Milner, 1992; Ungerleider and Mishkin, 1982).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational studies on the dorsal and ventral pathways.

claim: Both dorsal and ventral pathways process the same visual cues.
source: Contrary to initial speculation, both pathways process the same visual cues.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies showing shape, color, and motion selectivity in both pathways.

claim: Neurons with shape and color selectivity are found in both ventral and dorsal areas.
source: Neurons with shape and color selectivity are found not only in ventral areas but also in dorsal areas (Seidemann et al., 1999; Sereno and Maunsell, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies demonstrating shape and color selectivity in dorsal areas.

claim: Neurons with motion direction selectivity are found in both dorsal and ventral areas.
source: Likewise, neurons with motion direction selectivity are found not only in dorsal areas but also in ventral areas (Desimone and Schein, 1987; Li et al., 2013; Mountcastle et al., 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies demonstrating motion direction selectivity in ventral areas.

claim: Binocular disparity is the positional difference between images projected to the left and right eyes.
source: One of the most notable visual cues in this regard is binocular disparity, the positional difference between images projected to the left and right eyes.
evidence: This is a standard definition of binocular disparity in vision science.

claim: Binocular disparity is used for recognition of 3D objects, visually guided 3D action, and navigation through the 3D environment.
source: As a precise cue for stereoscopic depth, binocular disparity is used for many functions, including the recognition of 3D objects, visually guided 3D action (e.g., reaching, grasping, and vergence eye movement), and navigation through the 3D environment (e.g., moving through obstacles).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about the functional roles of binocular disparity in vision.

claim: The visual system processes binocular disparity along both the dorsal and ventral pathways.
source: As binocular disparity is used for both 'what' (object vision) and 'where' (spatial vision) functions, the visual system processes binocular disparity along both the dorsal and ventral pathways (Neri, 2005; Orban et al., 2006; Parker, 2007; Roe et al., 2012; Welchman, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies on disparity processing in both pathways.

claim: To encode binocular disparity faithfully, the visual system should identify corresponding visual features in left and right retinal images.
source: To encode binocular disparity faithfully in accordance with the geometry of the 3D world, the visual system should identify the corresponding visual features in left and right retinal images that originate from the same surface point in the 3D space (Julesz, 1971; Marr and Poggio, 1976; Marr and Poggio, 1979).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational work on the stereo correspondence problem.

claim: Anticorrelated random-dot stereograms (aRDSs) are used to probe the neuronal process for stereo correspondence.
source: A conventional method to probe the neuronal process for stereo correspondence is to measure the disparity selectivity for anticorrelated random-dot stereograms (aRDSs) (Chen et al., 2017; Cumming and Parker, 1997; Goncalves and Welchman, 2017; Janssen et al., 2003; Krug et al., 2004; Kumano et al., 2008; Nieder and Wagner, 2001; Ohzawa, 1998; Samonds et al., 2013; Takemura et al., 2001; Tanabe et al., 2004; Theys et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by numerous citations to previous studies using aRDSs to study stereo correspondence.

claim: In aRDSs, one eye image is contrast-reversed to eliminate the natural solution to the correspondence problem.
source: In aRDSs, one eye image is contrast-reversed to eliminate the natural solution to the correspondence problem; the natural solution requires the depth of the corresponding points to vary smoothly over space, but such a solution does not exist for aRDSs.
evidence: This is a standard explanation of how aRDSs work, based on established knowledge in vision science.

claim: Many V1 neurons falsely encode the disparity embedded in aRDSs.
source: Although the activity of many V1 neurons encodes binocular disparity, these neurons also falsely encode the disparity embedded in aRDSs (Cumming and Parker, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study demonstrating this property of V1 neurons.

claim: Simple computations akin to interocular cross-correlation explain the primitive disparity representation in V1.
source: Simple computations akin to interocular cross-correlation explain this primitive disparity representation (Ohzawa et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a foundational study on the disparity energy model.

claim: 83 disparity-selective neurons were recorded in MT.
source: We compared how neurons in MT and V4 responded to graded anticorrelation by examining the responses of 83 disparity-selective neurons in MT (monkey O, N = 32; monkey A, N = 51) and 78 disparity selective neurons in V4 (monkey O, N = 29; monkey I, N = 49).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the sample size from the experimental data.

claim: 78 disparity-selective neurons were recorded in V4.
source: We compared how neurons in MT and V4 responded to graded anticorrelation by examining the responses of 83 disparity-selective neurons in MT (monkey O, N = 32; monkey A, N = 51) and 78 disparity selective neurons in V4 (monkey O, N = 29; monkey I, N = 49).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the sample size from the experimental data.

claim: Disparity selectivity was determined from responses to cRDSs using a Kruskal-Wallis test with p<0.05.
source: Disparity selectivity was determined from the responses to cRDSs (Kruskal–Wallis test; p<0.05).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the statistical method used to determine disparity selectivity.

claim: The example MT neuron's response pattern was reminiscent of the correlation-based representation of disparity.
source: The change observed for the example MT neuron is reminiscent of the correlation-based representation of disparity: when the correlation level decreased from 100% to 0% (hmRDS), the tuning amplitude gradually decreased to almost zero (flat curve).
evidence: This claim is based on the observed data from a single example neuron shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The example V4 neuron's response pattern was closer to the match-based representation.
source: Compared to this MT example, the response pattern of the example V4 neuron was closer to the match-based representation: the tuning amplitude was noticeably retained at 0% correlation with a relatively unchanged tuning phase (shape).
evidence: This claim is based on the observed data from a single example neuron shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In MT, only 1.2% of neurons were disparity selective at -30% correlation.
source: The fraction was minimal at −30% correlation, where only one out of 83 MT neurons (1.2%) was disparity selective.
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of the MT population data.

claim: In MT, 25.3% of neurons were disparity selective at -100% correlation.
source: With further decrease from −30% to −100%, the fraction increased to 21/83 (25.3%).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of the MT population data.

claim: In MT, 75% of neurons inverted their tuning curves at -100% correlation.
source: Notably, significant fractions of neurons inverted their tuning curves at the two most negative correlation levels we tested (75% [62/83] and 78% [65/83] of neurons at the −100% and −70% correlation levels, respectively; p=3.8 × 10−6 and 1.1 × 10−7; H0: the fraction is 0.5; binomial test).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of the MT population data with binomial test.

claim: In MT, 78% of neurons inverted their tuning curves at -70% correlation.
source: Notably, significant fractions of neurons inverted their tuning curves at the two most negative correlation levels we tested (75% [62/83] and 78% [65/83] of neurons at the −100% and −70% correlation levels, respectively; p=3.8 × 10−6 and 1.1 × 10−7; H0: the fraction is 0.5; binomial test).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of the MT population data with binomial test.

claim: The V4 population data lacked the characteristic U-shaped pattern of correlation-based representation.
source: The V4 population data were markedly different from the MT data, entirely lacking the aforementioned characteristics of the correlation-based representation.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of population data shown in Figure 3B versus Figure 3A.

claim: In V4, the fraction of neurons with inverted tuning gradually increased with gradual anticorrelation but did not surpass the chance level.
source: The fraction of neurons with inverted tuning gradually increased with gradual anticorrelation but did not surpass the chance level (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of the V4 population data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The median area ratio was 0.50 in MT and significantly larger than 0.
source: In MT, the median area ratio was 0.50 and significantly larger than 0 (two-sided Wilcoxson signed-rank test, p=1.6 × 10−10).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of the area ratio distribution in MT.

claim: The median area ratio was 0.17 in V4 and significantly lower than that in MT.
source: In V4, it was 0.17 and significantly lower than that in MT (two-sided Mann–Whitney U-test, p=3.6 × 10−4).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis comparing area ratio distributions between MT and V4.

claim: The distribution of the amplitude ratio was indistinguishable between MT and V4.
source: The distribution of the amplitude ratio was indistinguishable between the two areas (Figure 5D–F). The median values were 0.32 and 0.30 for MT and V4, respectively (two-sided Mann–Whitney U-test, p=0.47).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical comparison of amplitude ratio distributions between MT and V4.

claim: The area ratio was positively correlated with the reflected symmetry phase in MT.
source: The area ratio was positively correlated with the reflected symmetry phase both in MT and V4 (Figure 6A,B; MT: rs = 0.41, p=1.4 × 10−3; V4: rs = 0.34, p=0.025).
evidence: This claim is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 6A with Spearman's correlation coefficient.

claim: The area ratio was positively correlated with the reflected symmetry phase in V4.
source: The area ratio was positively correlated with the reflected symmetry phase both in MT and V4 (Figure 6A,B; MT: rs = 0.41, p=1.4 × 10−3; V4: rs = 0.34, p=0.025).
evidence: This claim is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 6B with Spearman's correlation coefficient.

claim: The latency of disparity selectivity was 78 ms in MT and 101 ms in V4.
source: The latency was 78 ms in MT and 101 ms in V4 (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is based on fitting cumulative Gaussian functions to the time course of disparity selectivity.

claim: The peak sDDI was 0.18 in MT and 0.13 in V4.
source: The peak sDDI was 0.18 in MT and 0.13 in V4.
evidence: This claim is based on fitting cumulative Gaussian functions to the time course of disparity selectivity.

claim: In V4, the latency was 29% greater than in MT.
source: Thus, compared with MT, in V4 the latency was 29% greater and the strength was 28% lower.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of fitted parameters from the time course analysis.

claim: In V4, the strength of disparity selectivity was 28% lower than in MT.
source: Thus, compared with MT, in V4 the latency was 29% greater and the strength was 28% lower.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of fitted parameters from the time course analysis.

claim: The differences in latency and amplitude between MT and V4 were statistically significant.
source: The differences were statistically significant (p=0.0083 and p<1.0 × 10−4 for the latency and amplitude differences between MT and V4, respectively; 10,000 bootstrap resamples).
evidence: This claim is based on bootstrap statistical analysis of the fitted parameters.

claim: The mean eccentricity was 6.9° for MT and 9.0° for V4.
source: The mean eccentricity was 6.9° (s.d. = 3.3°) for MT and 9.0° (s.d. = 3.0°) for V4 in our data sets.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the measured eccentricity values from the experimental data.

claim: The response of the threshold energy model was more consistent with the match-based representation when the relative RF was smaller.
source: The response of the threshold energy model was more consistent with the match-based representation when the relative RF was smaller (i.e., when the eccentricity was smaller).
evidence: This claim is based on simulation results shown in Figure 9.

claim: The area ratio monotonically increased with the relative RF size in the threshold energy model.
source: The area ratio monotonically increased with the relative RF size, indicating that the models with smaller RFs represent binocular disparity in a more match-based manner compared to the models with larger RFs (Figure 9E).
evidence: This claim is based on simulation results shown in Figure 9E.

claim: MT might consist of two groups of neurons: one with the match-based representation and the other with the intermediate representation.
source: MT might consist of two groups of neurons: one with the match-based representation and the other with the intermediate representation (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the potentially bimodal distribution of area ratios in MT shown in Figure 5A.

claim: V4 lacked the intermediate group of neurons.
source: V4 lacked the intermediate group (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is based on the unimodal distribution of area ratios in V4 shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The fast and robust disparity signals in MT should be useful for rapid three-dimensional eye movements and urgent depth judgments.
source: The fast and robust disparity signals in MT should be useful for rapid three-dimensional eye movements (Masson et al., 1997) and urgent depth judgments in response to correlated stimuli.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the observed properties of MT neurons and a citation to a previous study on vergence eye movements.

claim: MT pathway quickly and robustly relays the correlation-based disparity signals to the behavioral stage.
source: We propose that MT pathway quickly and robustly relays the correlation-based disparity signals to the behavioral stage.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation based on the experimental findings about MT's disparity representation and signaling properties.

claim: The link between disparity-selective neurons in MT and perceptual judgment has been demonstrated extensively using a coarse depth task.
source: The use of MT's disparity signals should not be limited to visually guided actions, because the link between the disparity-selective neurons in MT and perceptual judgment has been demonstrated extensively using a coarse depth task (Chowdhury and DeAngelis, 2008; DeAngelis et al., 1998; Uka and DeAngelis, 2004) and a structure-from-motion task (Bradley et al., 1998; Dodd et al., 2001; Krug et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies demonstrating the link between MT activity and perceptual judgment.

claim: Human depth judgment exhibits a trace of the correlation-based disparity representation.
source: Human depth judgment does indeed exhibit a trace of the correlation-based disparity representation (e.g., reversed depth perception for aRDSs; Aoki et al., 2017; Tanabe et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous psychophysical studies.

claim: The inferred contribution of the correlation-based representation to perceived depth increases with the magnitude of stimulus disparity.
source: Moreover, the inferred contribution of the correlation-based representation to perceived depth increases with the magnitude of stimulus disparity (Doi et al., 2011) as well as with the stimulus pattern refresh rate (Doi et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous psychophysical studies.

claim: MT contributes to coarse, but not fine, depth judgment.
source: The magnitude effect is consistent with the finding that MT contributes to coarse, but not fine, depth judgment (Uka and DeAngelis, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study on MT's contribution to depth judgment.

claim: The disparity signals in MT drive the reflexive vergence eye movement via the medial superior temporal area.
source: We also suggest that the disparity signals in MT drive the reflexive vergence eye movement via the medial superior temporal area (Takemura et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a suggested interpretation based on the experimental findings and a citation to a previous study.

claim: For anticorrelation, the vergence eye movement responds in the opposite direction from stimulus disparity with a reduced amplitude.
source: For anticorrelation, the vergence eye movement responds in the opposite direction from stimulus disparity with a reduced amplitude (Masson et al., 1997), suggesting that the driving signal is intermediate between the match-based and correlation-based representations.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study on vergence eye movements.

claim: The vergence response can start to rise only 60-70 ms after the stimulus onset.
source: The vergence response can be very fast, starting to rise only 60–70 ms after the stimulus onset (Masson et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study on vergence eye movements.

claim: MT neurons represent the 'absolute' disparity of a stimulus, without being sensitive to the disparity of a reference plane.
source: Our suggestion is also consistent with the finding that MT neurons represent the 'absolute' disparity of a stimulus, without being sensitive to the disparity of a reference plane (Uka and DeAngelis, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study on MT's disparity representation.

claim: V4 is likely to be in the middle of the neural process of solving the binocular correspondence problem along the ventral pathway.
source: V4 is likely to be in the middle of the neural process of solving the binocular correspondence problem along the ventral pathway.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings that V4 neurons show intermediate properties between V1 and IT.

claim: The correspondence problem is not yet fully solved in the single-neuron activity in V4.
source: Consistent with this idea is the finding that the correspondence problem is not yet fully solved in the single-neuron activity we observed in V4.
evidence: This claim is based on the experimental finding that V4 neurons still show some disparity selectivity at negative correlations.

claim: V4 neurons have choice-predictive responses during a fine depth task.
source: First, V4 neurons have choice-predictive responses during a fine depth task (Shiozaki et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Microstimulation of a cluster of V4 neurons biases the judgment of fine depth in the way predicted from the response property of the stimulated cluster.
source: Second, microstimulation of a cluster of V4 neurons biases the judgment of fine depth in the way predicted from the response property of the stimulated cluster (Shiozaki et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: V4 neurons encode the 'relative' disparity between the center and surround of their RFs.
source: Lastly, V4 neurons encode the 'relative' disparity between the center and surround of their RFs, a property necessary for supporting stereoacuity and a precursor for fixation-depth-invariant representation of 3D objects (Umeda et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: V4 is involved in the encoding of 3D shape cues such as 3D slant.
source: This is broadly consistent with the finding that V4 is involved in the encoding of 3D shape cues such as 3D slant (Hegdé and Van Essen, 2005; Hinkle and Connor, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: All procedures were approved by the Animal Experiment Committee of Osaka University.
source: All procedures were approved by the Animal Experiment Committee of Osaka University (permit numbers: FBS-12–016 and FBS-13-003-1) and conformed to the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals issued by the National Institutes of Health, USA.
evidence: This is a direct statement about ethical approval for the study.

claim: Two Japanese monkeys were used for MT recording.
source: We used two Japanese monkeys (Macaca fuscata) for MT recording (Monkey O, male, weighing 8.5 kg; Monkey A, female, weighing 5.7 kg), and one Japanese monkey (Monkey O) and one rhesus monkey (Monkey I, Macaca mulatta, male, weighing 6.5 kg) for V4 recording.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the animals used in the study.

claim: One Japanese monkey and one rhesus monkey were used for V4 recording.
source: We used two Japanese monkeys (Macaca fuscata) for MT recording (Monkey O, male, weighing 8.5 kg; Monkey A, female, weighing 5.7 kg), and one Japanese monkey (Monkey O) and one rhesus monkey (Monkey I, Macaca mulatta, male, weighing 6.5 kg) for V4 recording.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the animals used in the study.

claim: Monkey O provided data sets for both MT and V4.
source: Monkey O provided data sets for both MT and V4.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data collection.

claim: The RDSs consisted of a central disk and a surrounding ring with no gap between them.
source: The RDSs consisted of a central disk and a surrounding ring with no gap between them.
evidence: This is a direct description of the stimulus structure.

claim: The central disk was positioned to cover the classical RF of a recorded neuron.
source: The central disk was positioned to cover the classical RF of a recorded neuron.
evidence: This is a direct description of the stimulus positioning.

claim: The dot density was 25%.
source: The dot density was 25%.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the stimulus parameter.

claim: Most MT neurons (65 out of 83) had their RFs in the lower visual field.
source: Most of our MT neurons (65 out of 83) had their RFs in the lower visual field; RFs of all of our V4 neurons (N = 78) were located in lower visual field.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the RF locations in the recorded sample.

claim: RFs of all V4 neurons were located in lower visual field.
source: Most of our MT neurons (65 out of 83) had their RFs in the lower visual field; RFs of all of our V4 neurons (N = 78) were located in lower visual field.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the RF locations in the recorded sample.

claim: There was no correlation between the area ratio and eccentricity in MT.
source: We found no correlation between the area ratio (our metric for disparity representation) and eccentricity either in MT (Spearman's correlation rs = −0.035, p=0.79) or in V4 (rs = −0.065, p=0.68).
evidence: This claim is based on correlation analysis of the experimental data.

claim: There was no correlation between the area ratio and eccentricity in V4.
source: We found no correlation between the area ratio (our metric for disparity representation) and eccentricity either in MT (Spearman's correlation rs = −0.035, p=0.79) or in V4 (rs = −0.065, p=0.68).
evidence: This claim is based on correlation analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The division of labor between the dorsal and ventral visual pathways may embody the tradeoff between rapid and robust transmission of sensory signals and complex computation needed to derive elaborate sensory representations.
source: Therefore, the division of labor between the dorsal and ventral visual pathways may embody the tradeoff between the rapid and robust transmission of sensory signals and the complex computation needed to derive elaborate sensory representations.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation that synthesizes the experimental findings into a broader theoretical framework.

claim: Vision related to action may depend more on the dorsal pathway because it benefits from rapid, robust sensory transmission.
source: For example, vision related to action may depend more on the dorsal pathway because it benefits from rapid, robust sensory transmission, and so does visual motion perception.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation that connects the experimental findings to broader theories of dorsal/ventral pathway function.

claim: The analyses of colors and objects may depend more on the ventral pathway because they require complex computations.
source: The analyses of colors and objects may depend more on the ventral pathway because they require complex computations.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation that connects the experimental findings to broader theories of dorsal/ventral pathway function.
